opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important and honestly most underrated problems in the field right now. Everyone talks about the models and the data, but the hard part is really the people and how they work together.

The way I think about it is that you can't just put a bunch of biologists in one room and a bunch of ML researchers in another and expect magic to happen when they occasionally meet. You end up with what I'd call a service relationship. The biologists treat the computational folks as a core facility, "here's my data, analyze it," or the ML people treat the wet lab as a data-generation factory. Neither of those produces anything truly new.

What you want is people who are bilingual, or at least conversational, in both. Not everyone has to be a world expert in both domains. That's rare and probably unrealistic. But you need people who can understand the other side's constraints. The ML researcher should get why an experiment takes three weeks, why it's noisy, why some measurements just aren't possible at scale. The biologist should get what makes a dataset useful for training, why you'd want negative data, why consistency and scale matter more than one beautiful figure.

At Arc, a lot of what we've tried to do is design the organization around that tight loop. Can you generate data specifically for model building, rather than repurposing data collected for other reasons? Can you take model predictions back into the lab quickly to test them? When that lab-in-the-loop cycle gets fast, the two cultures start to merge, because everyone is staring at the same results and feels ownership over the same outcomes.

Culture matters a lot too. Biology and ML have very different norms. ML moves fast, publishes on arXiv, iterates on benchmarks. Biology is slower and more careful, and for good reason, because the systems are messy and you get fooled easily. You want to keep the rigor of biology and the speed and engineering mindset of ML, without one side feeling like second-class citizens.

And frankly, a lot of it comes down to hiring for curiosity and humility. The best people at this interface are the ones who are genuinely excited to learn the other field, and who are comfortable saying "I don't know" in a room full of experts from a different discipline. If you get that right, the rest gets a lot easier.

r001.rationale: It says that world experts in both fields are rare and unrealistic, but does not compare the prevalence of people fluent in both with specialists in either field.

r002.rationale: It describes bilingual people as understanding each field’s constraints and helping the two cultures merge around shared outcomes, conveying a translator role that improves collaboration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that it's really hard, and most people who say they're doing it are actually doing something else, which is they've built a biology team and a machine learning team and they sit in the same building.

What we've tried to do at Arc, and what I think actually works, is you have to hire people who are willing to be a beginner again in the other field. That's the hard part. If you're a really good ML researcher, you've spent years building taste about what a good result looks like, what a good benchmark looks like, and biology violates all of that intuition. The data is noisy, the labels are often wrong, the "ground truth" came from an experiment someone ran in 2009 under conditions nobody wrote down. And conversely, if you're a biologist, you've been trained to think about mechanism, about one gene and one pathway, and then someone hands you a model with a billion parameters and tells you it's learning the genome and you have no way to evaluate whether that's real or not.

So the first thing we look for is people who are genuinely curious and a little bit uncomfortable. Not people who want to be the smartest person in the room about their own thing, but people who are excited to ask the stupid question in the other room.

The second thing, and I think this is underrated, is you need shared artifacts. For us that's been something like Evo, where the biologists and the ML people are literally staring at the same model, the same evaluations, the same weird failure modes. When a generative model produces a sequence and the biologists go, that's not a real protein, that doesn't fold, that's a conversation that wouldn't happen if they were in separate groups. The model becomes the common language. Same thing with Virtual Cell, where the question of what does it even mean for a cell model to be good is itself an interdisciplinary question. You can't answer it from either side alone.

And the third piece is just structural. Academic incentives really fight you on this. In a traditional lab, you get credit for being first author on a paper in your field, and the person who spent six months building the data pipeline or the wet lab assay that made the model possible doesn't get much. So we've tried to set up a place where the engineer who makes the training infrastructure work and the scientist who generates the perturbation data are treated as actually doing the science, not supporting it. If you don't fix that, people will self-sort back into their own tribes within a year.

The thing I keep coming back to is that biology is about to look a lot more like a computational discipline, in the sense that the rate-limiting step is shifting from can we measure this to can we make sense of what we measured. And I don't think you get there by having two separate cultures. You get there by making a third one, which is uncomfortable for everyone involved, but that discomfort is kind of the point.

r001.rationale: The response says it is hard to build an integrated team and values people willing to be beginners in the other field, but it does not state that people fluent in both fields are rarer than specialists.

r002.rationale: The response describes shared models as a common language for biologists and ML researchers, but does not identify people fluent in both fields as translators who make the team more effective.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to build around a shared problem, rather than around a collection of disciplines. You can hire excellent biologists and excellent machine learning researchers, but if everyone stays within their own vocabulary and their own definition of success, you don’t necessarily get an effective team.

What you want are people who have depth in something, but also enough curiosity and humility to ask basic questions in another field. A machine learning researcher should feel comfortable asking how an assay actually works. A biologist should feel comfortable asking what a model is learning and whether the benchmark captures something biologically meaningful.

That also means getting those people involved together at the beginning. If the interaction is simply, “We generated some data; now please analyze it,” you’ve missed an opportunity. The experimental design, the measurements you collect, and the modeling approach should inform one another.

And then you need a shared feedback loop: make a prediction, test it experimentally, understand where it failed, and use that to improve the next experiment and the next model. That gives the team something concrete to learn from together. Over time, you develop a shared language through doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses complementary specialists but does not say that people fluent in both fields are rarer than specialists.

r002.rationale: It describes cross-field curiosity and developing a shared language, but does not identify people fluent in both fields as translators who improve the broader team’s effectiveness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it starts with finding people who are curious enough to take another field seriously. You can put a biologist and a machine learning researcher next to each other, but that doesn’t automatically create an interdisciplinary team. They need a shared problem that neither can solve alone, and enough time together to develop a common language.

A lot of that happens in the details. What does a measurement actually mean? What variation is biological, and what comes from the assay? If a model makes a prediction, what experiment would tell us whether it learned something useful? Those questions require both perspectives from the beginning.

You also need people who can bridge disciplines, but you shouldn’t expect everyone to become an expert in everything. The goal is deep expertise with enough mutual understanding to challenge assumptions and build together. And culturally, people have to feel comfortable asking very basic questions. Often, those are the questions that expose an assumption everyone else has stopped noticing.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that people fluent in both fields are rarer than specialists.

r002.rationale: It says the team needs people who can bridge disciplines, but does not identify people fluent in both fields as translators who make the broader team more effective.
